strengths: Clear problem formulation with excellent motivation: effectively identifies the mismatch between ReID (general distinction) and MOT (sequence-specific distinction) objectives, with compelling visualizations

Strong empirical results on appearance-challenging benchmarks: 61.2 HOTA on DanceTrack (vs. 50.6 baseline) and exceptional 79.3 HOTA on SportsMOT (7.2 HOTA improvement over DiffMOT using identical ReID model)
Simple, elegant, and training-free solution: applies Fisher Linear Discriminant with closed-form solution, enabling practitioners to improve any pretrained ReID model without retraining

Comprehensive experimental validation: thorough ablations (Tables 5-8), fair baseline design isolating appearance contributions, multiple challenging datasets, and consistent zero-shot improvements across different encoders
Valuable methodological insights: temporal weighting of trajectory centroids (Section 3.3) is well-motivated for online tracking scenarios where recent features are more reliable
Good presentation: clear visualizations (especially Fig. 3 showing FLD superiority over PCA), transparent discussion of limitations, and reproducible experimental setup
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution applies classical Fisher Linear Discriminant (1938) to MOT; temporal weighting and knowledge integration are straightforward extensions without significant algorithmic innovation

Computational efficiency unresolved: 22.7 FPS is marginal for real-time requirements; CPU-based eigenvalue computation identified as bottleneck with no practical solution (GPU libraries lack generalized eigenvalue interface); this critical limitation relegated to appendix

Hyperparameter tuning contradicts training-free claim: multiple parameters (T, λ₀, α) require dataset-specific tuning (marked † in results); undermines practical simplicity and training-free narrative

Complete exclusion of position/motion information: while enabling clear ablations, this is a critical limitation; marginal MOT17 gains (63.5 vs 64.5 HOTA for DiffMOT) when linear motion dominates demonstrate limited applicability to realistic scenarios

Poor generalization to diverse object categories: TAO results show minimal improvements (+0.6-0.7 TETA vs +10+ on DanceTrack); advantage primarily for similar-appearance scenarios, limiting impact for general MOT

Insufficient theoretical justification: no formal analysis of why FLD's optimization objective is suitable for MOT; comparison with alternative tracking-specific criteria lacking; intuition provided but rigor insufficient

Knowledge Integration appears to be a patch: pure FLD (α=1) underperforms combined approach, suggesting systematic limitations (e.g., unreliable with ID misallocation) that require safeguards, reducing method elegance

Statistical rigor absent: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; single-run results without variance estimates; particularly concerning given dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning

Incomplete experimental analysis: limited failure case discussion; no analysis of performance vs sequence length or trajectory density; Oracle detection experiments show detection dominates, limiting practical relevance; insufficient explanation of why method excels for sports (Table 3) but not general objects (Table 4)

Code unavailability and reproducibility: abstract states 'code will be released at .' with incomplete URL; implementation details unclear (e.g., projection matrix update frequency); grid search parameters incompletely specified

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: The paper articulates a meaningful distinction between ReID task objectives (general discrimination) and MOT requirements (sequence-specific discrimination), with effective visualizations (Figure 1) supporting this motivation.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive ablations (Tables 5-8) systematically validate each component, and experiments across multiple diverse benchmarks (DanceTrack, MOT17, SportsMOT, TAO) demonstrate breadth.

Strong empirical results on specific scenarios: Substantial improvements on DanceTrack (+8.0 HOTA) and particularly on SportsMOT (+7.2 HOTA vs. DiffMOT using identical ReID model) show practical effectiveness in scenarios with high appearance similarity.
Zero-shot transfer capability: Demonstrated improvements with multiple zero-shot ReID models (Table 4) across different visual encoders, indicating robustness to feature source variation.
Training-free method: The approach requires no additional training and integrates cleanly into existing tracking pipelines, improving accessibility and deployment ease.
Well-executed experimental design for the baseline: The 'FastReID-MOT' naive tracker isolates the contribution of ReID enhancement, making the ablation studies clear and interpretable.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The core contribution applies Fisher Linear Discriminant Analysis (a 1938 classical method) to MOT. While the application is reasonable, the algorithmic innovation is minimal—treating trajectories as FLD classes is a straightforward adaptation of existing theory without substantial innovation.

Questionable experimental fairness: Comparisons with state-of-the-art methods (Tables 1-3) are problematic because the baseline deliberately excludes position information, while most SOTA methods integrate both appearance and motion. The superiority claimed is partly attributable to this design choice rather than the FLD contribution itself. Direct claim of 'superior tracking performance' relative to SOTA is misleading given different methodological assumptions.

Significant computational limitations: The method runs at only 22.7 FPS with 'nearly all additional latency' from eigenvalue decomposition (Appendix B.1). Proposed GPU speedups (4-10×) are speculative and unimplemented. This computational overhead is a practical barrier for real-time applications.

Inconsistent and dataset-dependent effectiveness: Minimal improvements on TAO (+0.6 HOTA, Table 4), where targets are naturally well-separated. The method's effectiveness is highly scenario-dependent, raising questions about generalization and when practitioners should apply it. This limitation receives insufficient discussion.

Hyperparameter sensitivity without principled selection: The method introduces hyperparameters (T, λ₀, α) with significant impact on performance (Tables 6-8). Notably, α requires adjustment across datasets (0.9 for standard cases, 0.5 for MASA), indicating lack of principled generalization. No methodology for selecting these on new datasets is provided.

Knowledge Integration design is ad-hoc: Section 3.4's weighted fusion of original and projected similarities (Eq. 10) lacks theoretical justification. Why weighted sum rather than other fusion approaches? The choice appears to be an engineering hack optimized post-hoc rather than a principled design, with limited exploration in ablations (Table 8 only tests α ∈ [0.6, 1.0]).

Insufficient analysis of failure modes and edge cases: No discussion of when FLD projection degrades performance, behavior early in sequences with limited history, or handling of ID switches. The paper lacks depth in understanding method limitations.

Missing comparisons with related methods: No performance comparison with LDA (closely related to FLD), only visual comparison in Figure 4. Limited justification for why FLD specifically is superior to other discriminative projection methods. Alternative subspace learning approaches are not explored.

Position information omission undermines practical relevance: The deliberate exclusion of position information (Sec. 4.2: 'to seek insightful analysis rather than concentrating on tedious engineering details') is a significant design choice that limits practical impact. While this aids clarity of ablation studies, it creates an artificial setting that doesn't reflect real MOT deployment.

Inconsistent theoretical development: Section 3.2 treats each trajectory as a class for FLD, but the classical FLD assumption of well-defined class structure may not hold in online tracking where trajectory assignments are uncertain and evolve over time. This fundamental mismatch is not addressed.

Incomplete reproducibility: The code URL in the abstract is blank ('The code will be released at .'), and several hyperparameter choices require dataset-specific tuning without clear guidelines. Zero-shot results use adjusted α (0.5 vs. 0.9), suggesting generalization challenges.

Weak justification for temporal-shifted centroid: While Table 7 validates that temporal weighting helps, the exponential decay formulation (λ₀)^(t') is presented without ablation of alternative schemes or theoretical motivation. The choice appears empirically driven rather than principled.

TAO results suggest limited scope: The minimal TETA improvement (+0.7 on TAO validation, Table 4) in a general multi-object tracking scenario suggests the method's value is limited to constrained settings with similar appearances, narrowing its impact for the broader MOT community.

strengths: Clear motivation identifying the mismatch between ReID and MOT objectives, effectively illustrated with feature space visualizations (Fig. 1)
Elegant and practical approach using FLD with closed-form solution, enabling training-free application to each sequence
Thorough experimental validation: comprehensive ablations (Tables 5-8), multiple benchmarks with complementary characteristics, and zero-shot transfer experiments demonstrating generalization
Strong empirical results, particularly on DanceTrack and SportsMOT (+7.2 HOTA improvement over DiffMOT with identical ReID model), demonstrating practical value
Well-designed baseline (single-stage, feature-only tracker) that cleanly isolates the contribution of the proposed method without confounding factors
Thoughtful design refinements including temporal-shifted trajectory centroid and knowledge integration, both validated with ablations
Effective presentation with clear writing and illustrative figures (especially Fig. 3 comparing FLD vs. PCA projections)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: FLD is a classical 1938 technique; contribution is primarily an engineering insight rather than a novel algorithm or method
Inconsistent improvements across benchmarks: slightly behind on MOT17 (63.5 vs. 64.5 for DiffMOT), minimal gains on TAO (+0.6-0.7 TETA), suggesting dataset-dependent benefits that limit generality

Hyperparameter tuning requirement despite 'training-free' framing: method requires dataset-specific tuning of T, λ₀, α (Tables 6-8 show 3+ HOTA sensitivity), and paper explicitly states adjusting hyperparameters across datasets
Practical speed limitation: 22.7 FPS achieved; CPU-based eigendecomposition is bottleneck; potential 4-10× GPU speedup is speculative and not realized, affecting real-world deployment viability

Limited comparison among feature-based methods: primarily compares against motion-based and hybrid approaches; only brief comparisons with QDTrack and ContrasTR weaken claims about feature space optimization
Ignores position information entirely, making the tracker somewhat artificial; integration with motion cues not explored, limiting practical applicability to real MOT systems
Theoretical justification incomplete: lacks analysis of why FLD is optimal for MOT specifically; no exploration of alternative discriminant methods or theoretical guarantees
Modest zero-shot improvements (Table 4): consistent but incremental gains (+2-3 HOTA), suggesting limited benefit when applied across different domains or ReID models

strengths: Well-motivated conceptual insight: Identifies fundamental mismatch between generic ReID (open-set) and MOT requirements (closed-set discrimination within videos), with clear visualization and empirical validation showing strong correlation between discriminability and tracking performance

Strong empirical results on appearance-heavy benchmarks: Achieves state-of-the-art on SportsMOT as ReID-only tracker (80.8 HOTA, surpassing hybrid methods) and significant improvements on DanceTrack (+10.7-14.4 AssA), validating the core hypothesis

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation: Tests across 6 major benchmarks, diverse visual backbones, multiple tracker architectures, with detailed ablation studies (Tables 5-8) and meaningful comparison between supervised and history-aware FLD approaches (Table 9)
Practical training-free approach: No model retraining required enables immediate integration with existing systems; easy to apply to diverse trackers and ReID models

Thoughtful design addressing real tracking challenges: Temporal weighting (Sec 4.2) handles appearance evolution, knowledge integration (Sec 4.3) balances specialization with robustness to tracking errors and newborn objects
Honest treatment of limitations: Comprehensive appendices (C-D) transparently discuss restricted gains on hybrid/E2E trackers, performance saturation on certain benchmarks, and computational overhead
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Fisher LDA is a classical 1936 technique; application to MOT is straightforward once motivated. Contribution is conceptual rather than algorithmic, with no novel mathematical formulations or technical innovations

Highly inconsistent cross-benchmark performance: Excellent gains on DanceTrack/SportsMOT (+10-15% AssA) but only marginal on MOT17 (+3.2 AssA) and TAO (+0.6-0.7 TETA). Improvements concentrate on two specialized benchmarks with uniform appearance, suggesting specialization rather than generality. Performance diminishes on balanced benchmarks

Significant computational overhead without practical solution: 2.2× slowdown (22.7 vs 46.5 FPS) severely limits real-time deployment for stated applications (autonomous driving, surveillance). GPU acceleration remains unimplemented and relegated to future work despite being fundamental for practical use

Limited improvements on state-of-the-art methods: Gains diminish to +2-4 HOTA on hybrid-based trackers; cannot be applied to leading E2E methods (MOTIP, SambaMOTR). This substantially reduces impact on modern tracking research despite conceptual merit

Questionable robustness to tracking errors: Method relies on potentially erroneous historical labels; knowledge integration (α=0.9) gives only 10% weight to specialized space as band-aid fix. Limited analysis of error propagation when early tracking is poor. Supervised FLD comparison (Table 9) underdeveloped, leaving core robustness assumptions unexplained

Specialization to ReID-heavy scenarios: Performance gains bounded by ReID quality; smaller improvements on general MASA backbone vs. DanceTrack-specific models. Method effectiveness diminishes as ReID models improve, limiting long-term utility

Borderline motivation for component choices: δ₁₀₀₀ metric is ad-hoc without sensitivity analysis. Why 1000 worst samples vs. other percentiles? Hyperparameter tuning (Tables 6-8) shows non-trivial variations despite robustness claims; default settings transferred across datasets without per-benchmark optimization

Limited scope of baselines and E2E discussion: Comparisons primarily with 2-3 year old trackers (acknowledged in Appendix D). While systematic analysis justified, weakens SOTA claims. Cannot be applied to emerging E2E paradigm despite being the research direction for MOT

strengths: Well-motivated observation with empirical validation: The paper clearly identifies that ReID features trained for open-set identification may be suboptimal for closed-set MOT, supported by the δ₁₀₀₀ discriminability metric and correlation analysis.

Thorough and rigorous experimental evaluation: Comprehensive testing on multiple benchmarks (DanceTrack, SportsMOT, TAO, MOT17, MOT20), integration with diverse tracker types, detailed ablations (Tables 5-9), oracle experiments, and honest reporting of dataset-specific limitations.

Methodologically sound comparisons: Supervised FLD baseline comparison (Table 9) validates the sequence-specific optimization insight; PCA comparison (Table 5) justifies the FLD choice; incremental ablations isolate component contributions.
Practical utility: Training-free method with closed-form solution that is easy to implement and integrate into existing ReID-based trackers without requiring model retraining.

Honest discussion of limitations: The paper forthrightly addresses inability to apply to end-to-end methods, modest gains on hybrid trackers, poor performance on naturally diverse datasets (MOT17), and 50% FPS reduction.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Applies the classical 1938 Fisher Linear Discriminant method with historical trajectory labels as classes. The core contribution is straightforward once the problem is framed, lacking theoretical analysis or methodological innovation.

Fundamentally restricted scope and applicability: Cannot be applied to end-to-end MOT methods which increasingly dominate the field; provides minimal gains (2-4 HOTA) on hybrid trackers; primarily effective only on ReID-only trackers, an increasingly marginal subfield in MOT research.

Highly dataset-dependent performance: Strong improvements on DanceTrack/SportsMOT (+8-11 HOTA) where targets have similar appearances, but minimal gains on MOT17 (+2.0 HOTA with naturally diverse pedestrians) and TAO (+0.6-0.7 TETA with diverse categories). Method appears to exploit dataset-specific biases rather than provide general advancement.

Computational efficiency penalty: ~50% FPS reduction (46.5→22.7) due to CPU-based eigenvalue computation, limiting practical deployment despite being 'near real-time'. Authors acknowledge this falls beyond scope but it is a significant practical limitation.

Methodological concerns with label propagation: Method assumes historical trajectory assignments are correct but does not thoroughly analyze how tracking errors propagate into the projection matrix; limited treatment of performance degradation for newborn objects not in the transformation space.

Ad-hoc design choices and inconsistent robustness claims: δ₁₀₀₀ metric lacks justification; Fig. 2a shows substantial variance in correlation; Table 8 demonstrates sensitivity to fusion coefficient α despite robustness claims; hyperparameter selection via grid search risks overfitting to specific benchmarks.

Questionable experimental framing: Built custom FastReID-MOT baseline rather than using established trackers; 'state-of-the-art' claims on SportsMOT apply only to ReID-only trackers while excluding E2E methods; hyperbolic language ('dramatically enhances,' 'compelling evidence') for modest improvements.

Missing critical analyses: No investigation of performance vs. track age; limited failure case analysis; restricted exploration of dimensionality reduction alternatives beyond PCA; insufficient comparison with more recent tracking methods (~2 years old); unexplored applicability to learnable/adaptive variants.

strengths: Well-motivated insight distinguishing MOT (closed-set, sequence-specific) from general ReID (open-set, universal), with rigorous empirical validation via δ1000 correlation analysis
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (DanceTrack, SportsMOT, TAO, MOT17, MOT20), visual backbones, and tracker architectures with extensive ablations
Strong empirical results on primary benchmarks: +10.6 HOTA on DanceTrack, +11.6 HOTA on SportsMOT with new SOTA for ReID-only methods; consistent improvements across diverse visual encoders

Elegant and practical training-free method: applying FLD with history-aware labeling is applicable to any ReID extractor without retraining; Table 9 effectively validates importance of sequence-specific vs. cross-video information

Insightful ablation studies systematically verify components (history length T, temporal decay λ₀, integration coefficient α); oracle experiments isolate feature transformation effects from detection noise
Effective visualizations and analysis demonstrating feature space improvements (Figures 2b, 4, 7) and clear presentation of the core problem and solution
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward application of classical FLD method with history-based labeling; incremental innovation beyond the conceptual insight

Inconsistent applicability across datasets severely undermines generality claims: MOT17 (+2.0 HOTA only, due to inherent pedestrian discriminability), TAO (~0.6-0.7 marginal gains with diverse object categories); method tailored to appearance-homogeneous scenarios
Significant computational overhead (22.7 FPS vs 46.5 FPS baseline, ~2× slowdown) with no practical solution provided; acknowledged CPU bottleneck in eigenvalue computation remains unresolved

Limited effectiveness on hybrid-based trackers (gains: +6.4 HOTA OC-SORT-ReID, +1.2 HOTA Hybrid-SORT-ReID); motion-prioritizing hybrid designs limit ReID branch impact, problematic since most practical trackers use hybrid approaches
Inapplicable to end-to-end MOT methods; cannot extend to emerging transformer-based approaches representing the future direction of the field

Hyperparameter selection weakens 'training-free' claim: results with dataset-specific fine-tuning (†) show consistent improvements over defaults (e.g., 58.6→61.2 HOTA on DanceTrack), requiring additional tuning burden

Insufficient analysis of failure modes and error propagation: limited discussion beyond MOT17; impact of accumulated tracking errors on FLD matrix construction not rigorously validated; δ1000 threshold selection lacks justification
Limited comparison with related sequence-adaptation methods [22, 8, 30, 6, 52, 20]; direct comparisons absent, with only broad tracker-level comparisons provided
